title: Why English Is Full of Latin and Greek
description: Four layers of borrowing, the doublets they left behind, and how to take a word apart

concepts.title: Four Layers of Borrowing
concepts.contentHtml:
English began as the Germanic speech of Angles, Saxons and Jutes who settled in Britain from the 5th century CE, and its core is still theirs: the, and, house, eat, mother, water. Even before the migration these peoples had picked up a few Latin trade words on the Roman frontier, probably including the ancestors of street (strata), wine (vinum) and cheese (caseus). Christian missionaries, arriving from 597 CE, added church and learning words, among them school.

The second layer came with the Norman Conquest of 1066. For about three centuries England's rulers spoke French, and a commonly repeated estimate holds that some 10,000 French words entered Middle English, most still in use. French had grown out of spoken Latin, so this layer is Latin worn smooth by centuries of everyday speech: royal, court, justice, beef.

The third layer was deliberate. Renaissance scholars of the 16th and 17th centuries borrowed straight from classical texts, and critics mocked the results as "inkhorn terms," after the horn that held a writer's ink. Thomas Wilson's Arte of Rhetorique (1553) printed a parody letter stuffed with words such as ingent (huge), which duly died. Many words that critics branded as inkhorn terms stuck: capacity, encyclopedia, meditate, strenuous.

The fourth layer is still being laid, as scientists build new words from Greek and Latin parts. In the late 1770s Antoine Lavoisier named oxygen from Greek for "acid-producer," because he wrongly believed every acid contained it; the name outlived the theory. Richard Owen coined dinosaur in 1842 from deinos "terrible, fearfully great" and sauros "lizard."

concepts.title: Counting the Layers, and Their Doublets
concepts.contentHtml:
How much of English is borrowed depends on what you count. A frequently cited computer survey by Thomas Finkenstaedt and Dieter Wolff (1973), run over the entries of the third edition of the Shorter Oxford Dictionary, sorted them as roughly 28 percent French, 28 percent Latin, 25 percent Germanic and 5 percent Greek. Other studies give other figures, and a dictionary count weighs a rare word like tergiversate the same as the. Count running speech instead and the picture flips: the most frequent words are overwhelmingly native Germanic.

The layers left English with sets of near-synonyms sorted by register. Kingly is a native formation, royal came through Old French, and regal is a learned borrowing that kept its Latin shape. In the same way rise, mount and ascend, or ask, question and interrogate, climb from plain to formal. The native word usually sounds warmest, the French one courtly, the Latin one official or technical.

Royal and regal are also a doublet: one Latin word, regalis, borrowed twice. The French route wore it down; the scholarly route left it intact. English has many such pairs. Loyal and legal both come from legalis, sure and secure from securus, frail and fragile from fragilis, count and compute from computare. The oddest pair is blame, Old French's worn-down form of Late Latin blasphemare "to revile," and blaspheme, the same verb borrowed again later with its shape intact.

concepts.title: Taking a Word Apart
concepts.contentHtml:
Most Latin and Greek words in English split into a prefix, a root and a suffix. Incredible is in- "not" + cred- "believe" + -ible "able to be": not able to be believed. Transmission is trans- "across" + miss- "send" + -ion "the act of." The root carries the meaning, the prefix steers it, and the suffix decides whether the result is a noun, verb or adjective.

Two habits of Latin hide the pieces. First, prefixes assimilate: their last consonant changes to match the sound after it, which is easier to say. In- stays in inactive but becomes im- in impossible, il- in illegal and ir- in irregular. Ad- "to, toward" melts into accept (ad + capere), affect (ad + facere), attract (ad + trahere) and assist. A doubled consonant after an initial a- is often the fingerprint of ad-.

Second, Latin verbs come with two stems, one from the present and one from the past participle, and English borrowed both. Mittere "send," participle missus, gives transmit and transmission, submit and submission. Capere "take," participle captus, gives capture; inside compounds its vowel shifted, so recipere gives recipient and reception. Words that came through French were smoothed again to -ceive: receive, deceive, conceive, perceive. Even recipe belongs here. It is the Latin command "take!", which physicians wrote at the head of prescriptions and which survives in the pharmacist's Rx.

title: Numbers, Places and Sizes
description: Greek and Latin counting roots, months that lost their places, and the roots of position

concepts.title: Two Ways to Count
concepts.contentHtml:
English keeps two sets of number roots, one Greek and one Latin, and often uses both for the same idea. A four-footed animal is a tetrapod in Greek (tetra + pous, pod- "foot") and a quadruped in Latin (quadru- + pes, ped-). A five-sided figure is a pentagon, but five musicians are a quintet.

  • one: Greek mono- (monologue), Latin uni- (unicycle)
  • two: di- (dioxide), bi- (biennial)
  • four: tetra- (tetrahedron), quadr- (quadrilateral)
  • five: penta- (pentathlon), quinque-, quint- (quintuplet)
  • ten: deca- (decathlon), dec- (decimal)
  • hundred: hecto- (hectare), cent- (century)
  • thousand: kilo- (kilometer), mille (millennium)

The metric system, adopted in France in 1795, turned the doubling into a rule: Greek prefixes for multiples (deca-, hecto-, kilo-), Latin for fractions (deci-, centi-, milli-). A kilometer is a thousand meters and a millimeter a thousandth of one. Kilo- itself is an irregular French formation from Greek khilioi "thousand."

Number roots in animal names are approximate. A centipede ("hundred feet") has between 15 and 191 pairs of legs, always an odd number of pairs, so never exactly a hundred legs. Millipedes ("thousand feet") fell short too until 2021, when researchers described Eumillipes persephone, from deep underground in Western Australia, with 1,306 legs.

concepts.title: Months Out of Place
concepts.contentHtml:
September, October, November and December mean "seventh," "eighth," "ninth" and "tenth" month, from Latin septem, octo, novem and decem. They are now the 9th to 12th months because the Roman count of months once began in March. Roman tradition credited Romulus with a ten-month calendar and King Numa with adding January and February. Those stories are legend, but the month names themselves show that the numbering once started in spring.

The rest of the record is political. Quintilis, the "fifth month," was renamed Julius after Julius Caesar in 44 BCE, and Sextilis, the "sixth," became Augustus in 8 BCE in honor of the first emperor. January 1 became the start of the official year in 153 BCE, when the Senate had the new consuls take office then instead of in March, apparently so that a commander could reach a war in Spain sooner. The old numbers stayed on the later months anyway.

Other number words have drifted. Noon comes from Latin nona hora, the "ninth hour" counted from sunrise, about 3 p.m. By around the 14th century it had moved to midday; one explanation is that church fasts ended at that hour, but nobody is sure. Decimate comes from a Roman punishment in which one soldier in ten, chosen by lot, was killed to punish a whole unit. Plutarch says Crassus used it, in 72 or 71 BCE, on men who had fled from Spartacus. English first used the verb in that sense around 1600, before it broadened to "destroy a large part of."

concepts.title: Where Things Are: Position Roots
concepts.contentHtml:
Greek mesos and Latin medius both mean "middle." Mesopotamia is Greek for the land "between the rivers," the Tigris and Euphrates (mesos + potamos "river"). The Mesozoic era, named by the geologist John Phillips in 1840, is "middle life," between the Paleozoic ("old life") and Cenozoic ("new life"). Latin mediterraneus meant "inland, in the middle of the land"; only in late Latin did it name the sea.

Many position roots come in Greek and Latin pairs. "Around" is peri- or circum-: a perimeter is a "measure around," a circumference a "carrying around." "Under" is hypo- or sub-, and "over, beyond" is hyper- or super-. Sometimes English keeps both. A hypodermic needle and a subcutaneous injection both go "under the skin," one in Greek (derma), one in Latin (cutis). Supersonic means faster than sound, while hypersonic, a 20th-century coinage, came to mean more than about five times faster.

A few more are worth memorizing. Greek para- "beside" gives parallel. Greek meta- "after, beyond, changed" gives metamorphosis, a change of form; metaphysics probably began as an editor's label for the books placed after the Physics in Aristotle's collected works, later read as "beyond the physical." Latin inter- "between" and intra- "within" split cleanly: Jeremy Bentham coined international in a book printed in 1780, while an intravenous drip goes into a vein.

title: Verb Roots: Being, Making, Leading, Carrying
description: Five Latin verbs, esse, posse, facere, ducere and ferre, behind hundreds of English words

concepts.title: Being and Being Able: esse and posse
concepts.contentHtml:
Latin esse "to be" hides in common words. Absent is from abesse, "to be away"; present from praeesse, "to be before, be at hand." Interest is Latin interest, "it is between," which meant "it matters." The verb is as irregular as English be: its future participle futurus, "about to be," came from a different root and gave us future. Essence was a deliberate coinage. Latin lacked a word for the Greek philosophers' ousia "being," and Seneca credited Cicero with inventing essentia, though Quintilian named another author.

Latin posse "to be able" grew from potis "able, powerful" plus esse, roughly "to be master," though exactly how the forms merged is disputed. Its participle potens gives potent, impotent, omnipotent ("all-able") and potentate. Late Latin potentialis gives potential: what something is able to become but is not yet. Possible is from possibilis, "that can be done." Power took the long road, through Old French povoir from a spoken Latin reshaping, *potere. Possess is probably potis + sedere "to sit": to sit as master of something.

The word posse made its own journey. English legal Latin used posse comitatus, "the force of the county," for the men a sheriff could call out to help enforce the law. By the 1640s posse alone meant an armed band, and after American Westerns made the sheriff's posse familiar, the 20th century turned it into slang for a gang or a group of friends.

concepts.title: Making: facere
concepts.contentHtml:
Latin facere "to make, to do" appears as fac- and fact-, and inside compounds as -fic- and -fect-. Spot these and many words open up: perfect (made thoroughly), effect, efficient, infect, artifact (made by skill).

A fact was first a deed. Latin factum means "a thing done," and when the word entered English in the 1530s it meant an action, in the 16th and 17th centuries often a crime, which is why an accomplice can still be an accessory "after the fact." The modern sense, "something known to be true," dates from the 1630s. Factory drifted too. In the 1580s it meant a trading station abroad run by merchants' agents, called factors, and only from the 1610s a building for making goods.

Manufacture is manu "by hand" + factura "a making." It entered English in the 1560s for something made by hand; today it usually means made by machine. Difficult goes back to difficilis, apparently dis- + facilis "easy to do," itself from facere; why dis- works as a negative here is an old puzzle that dictionaries still discuss. Office is a shortening of opificium, "work-doing."

The verb-making suffix -fy is facere again, through French -fier from Latin -ficare. To magnify is to make great, to simplify to make simple, to terrify to make afraid. English still builds new verbs this way, as in gentrify, made from gentry.

concepts.title: Leading and Carrying: ducere and ferre
concepts.contentHtml:
Latin ducere "to lead" (stems duc- and duct-) gives the noun dux "leader," which became duke in French and English and doge in Venice. Its compounds are maps of direction: to conduct is to lead together, produce to lead forth, reduce to lead back, seduce (se- "aside") to lead astray. An aqueduct is a ductus, a channel, for aqua, water.

Educate needs care. It comes from educare "to rear, bring up," a verb related to educere "to lead out." Speeches often claim that education literally means drawing out what is already inside the pupil. That argument leans on the related verb rather than the word's direct source, and the 19th-century Century Dictionary rejected it outright.

Latin ferre "to carry, bear" is stranger. Its past participle latus comes from a different root, the one behind tollere "to lift," and English borrowed both halves. So pairs that look unrelated are one verb: transfer and translate (carry across), refer and relate (carry back), confer and collate (bring together). A legislator is Latin legis lator, the "proposer," literally the bearer, of a law. Greek pherein and English bear descend from the same Indo-European root as ferre, and Greek metaphora, a "carrying over," is the exact counterpart of Latin translatio.

title: Body, Medicine and the Clinic
description: Heart, head and skin roots, the suffixes that build a diagnosis, and four words with case histories

concepts.title: Heart, Head and Skin
concepts.contentHtml:
Medicine names the body twice, in Greek and in Latin. The heart is Greek kardia and Latin cor, cord-. The Greek gives the clinical words: cardiac, cardiology, electrocardiogram. The Latin gives the emotional ones. A cordial welcome is heartfelt, and a cordial was first a medicine, food or drink meant to stimulate the heart. Courage came through French from the same root, and to record once meant to learn by heart, from Latin recordari "to call to mind," with the heart as the seat of memory.

The head is Greek kephale and Latin caput, capit-. Encephalitis unpacks to en "in" + kephale "head" + -itis "inflammation": the brain, the thing inside the head, is inflamed. Hydrocephalus is "water head." An octopus is a cephalopod, "head-foot," because its arms grow from its head. On the Latin side a captain is the head man, a chapter is a "little head" or heading (capitulum), and a capital crime is one that costs the offender his head, that is, his life.

Skin is Greek derma and Latin cutis. Dermatology studies it, the epidermis lies upon it, and a pachyderm such as an elephant is "thick-skinned." The Latin gives cutaneous and subcutaneous. A good habit with any medical word: find the body part first, then read what the prefix and suffix do to it.

concepts.title: Building a Diagnosis, and the ped- Trap
concepts.contentHtml:
Clinical words are assembled from standard Greek parts. -itis marks inflammation. It began as an ordinary adjective ending: arthritis was short for nosos arthritis, "disease of the joints," with the word for disease understood. -ectomy (ek "out" + tome "cutting") is surgical removal; -tomy alone is a cut into something. The same verb temnein "to cut" gives anatomy, "cutting up," and atom, the "uncuttable" particle of Greek philosophers. -ology (logos "word, account") is the study of something. Hybrids are common: appendicitis (1886) puts a Greek suffix on Latin appendix.

Greek iatros means "healer," and here lies the classic trap. Pediatrics is pais, paid- "child" + healing. Podiatry, coined in the US around 1914 to replace chiropody ("hand-foot"), is pous, pod- "foot" + healing. Latin pes, ped- also means "foot" and gives pedestrian, pedal, pedicure and impede, from impedire, to shackle the feet.

So ped- can mean child (Greek) or foot (Latin). A pedagogue was a Greek paidagogos, a household slave who escorted a boy to school and supervised him. Orthopedics looks like "straight feet" but means "straight child": Nicolas Andry coined French orthopédie in his 1741 book on preventing and correcting deformities in children, from orthos "straight" and paidion "child." British spelling keeps a clue, since paediatric and orthopaedic preserve the Greek vowel.

concepts.title: Four Diagnoses with Case Histories
concepts.contentHtml:
Muscle is Latin musculus, "little mouse." The usual explanation is that a flexing muscle, the biceps especially, looked like a mouse moving under the skin. Greek used the same image: mys meant both mouse and muscle and gives the prefix myo-. The shellfish mussel comes from the same Latin word.

Hysteria comes from Greek hystera "womb." Some Hippocratic texts and a passage in Plato's Timaeus describe a womb that moves through the body and causes illness, an idea later doctors kept alive for centuries. But the noun hysteria is a modern medical coinage, recorded in English from 1801, and the historian Helen King has argued that ancient medicine had no single disease of that name; the Greek pedigree was partly a later construction that lent the diagnosis authority.

Nostalgia was a diagnosis before it was a mood. In 1688 Johannes Hofer, a medical student at Basel, joined Greek nostos "return home" and algos "pain" to name the condition German speakers called Heimweh, homesickness. Doctors linked it especially with Swiss mercenaries serving far from home and believed it could end in fever and death.

Vaccine is from Latin vacca "cow." Edward Jenner's 1798 Inquiry described protecting people against smallpox with material from cowpox, which he called variolae vaccinae, "smallpox of the cow." In 1881 Louis Pasteur stretched vaccination to cover his own protective inoculations against animal diseases, a choice usually described as homage to Jenner.

title: Fossil Stories in Everyday Words
description: Five words with history inside them, and one famous story the evidence does not support

concepts.title: Candidate and Companion
concepts.contentHtml:
A Roman seeking office walked the Forum in a toga candida, a toga bleached and probably rubbed with chalk to make it brilliant white. The man inside it was candidatus, "dressed in white," and English took candidate from that around 1600. The root is candere "to shine," which also gives candle, incandescent and candid, which meant "white" in the 1620s and "frank" by the 1670s. Roman campaigning left another word. Ambitio meant "a going around," the candidate's rounds to solicit votes, and in early English ambition was always a fault, grouped with pride and vainglory.

Companion is from Late Latin companio, built from com "with" and panis "bread": someone you share bread with, a messmate. It is first recorded in the Lex Salica, the law code of the Franks, usually dated to around 500 CE. Many scholars think it translates a Germanic word, since Gothic had gahlaiba "messmate," literally "with-loaf."

The same Germanic word for loaf sits inside two English titles. Lord is Old English hlaford, contracted from hlafweard, "loaf-guardian," and lady is hlaefdige, apparently "loaf-kneader." When companion arrived from French around 1300, it pushed out the Old English gefera, "traveling companion." The bread is still there in company and accompany, and in pantry, first a storeroom for bread.

concepts.title: School and Electric
concepts.contentHtml:
Greek skhole meant "leisure, spare time." For a free Greek man the best use of leisure was discussion and study, so the word came to mean a lecture and then the place where lectures were given. Aristotle put the old priority plainly: "we are busy so that we may have leisure." His verb for being busy is built on "no leisure," and Latin made the same move with negotium "business," from neg- + otium "leisure," the source of negotiate. Latin borrowed schola, and Old English took scol from it. A school of fish is a different word, from Middle Dutch schole "troop, multitude."

Greek elektron meant amber, the fossil tree resin that, when rubbed, picks up chaff and dust. A tradition credits Thales of Miletus, in the 6th century BCE, with noticing this, but it rests on a single remark by Diogenes Laertius, writing some 800 years later. In 1600 the English physician William Gilbert, in his book De Magnete, coined the Latin adjective electricus, "amber-like," for substances that attract light objects when rubbed. Sir Thomas Browne used electricity in English in 1646.

The chain kept going. In 1891 the Irish physicist George Johnstone Stoney proposed electron as the name for a natural unit of electric charge. After J. J. Thomson identified the particle in 1897, which he called a corpuscle, the name electron won out. The particle that carries every current is, at bottom, named for amber.

concepts.title: Salary: A Story Worth Checking
concepts.contentHtml:
Latin salarium really does come from sal "salt": it is a noun formed from the adjective salarius, "of salt." In the early Roman Empire it meant a regular stipend or allowance; Tacitus uses it for the payment customarily offered to a proconsul. English took it as salary around 1300. Up to that point the etymology is solid.

The popular story goes further: Roman soldiers were paid in salt, or given money to buy it, so a salary was "salt money." No ancient source says so. The phrase salarium argentum "salt money" is a modern reconstruction, not attested Latin. The usual prooftext is Pliny the Elder, who, in a chapter praising salt (Natural History 31.89), says only that the word salarium comes from salt and mentions an undefined link between salt and military honors. Merriam-Webster's editors trace the soldier story to 18th- and 19th-century Latin dictionaries copying one another, and the classicist Peter Gainsford has called it a modern myth. Other guesses, such as a tie to the Via Salaria, the salt road into Rome, are just as unproven.

The safe statement is that salary contains salt and nobody knows exactly why. Salt's other descendants are clearer. Salad is from herba salata, "salted greens"; sauce and salsa from salsus "salted"; sausage from salsicius, "prepared by salting." The idiom "worth one's salt" is not recorded before the 19th century, so it cannot serve as evidence either.

title: Traps, Hybrids and False Roots
description: Lookalike roots, words built from two languages, and popular etymologies that fail the evidence

concepts.title: Lookalikes
concepts.contentHtml:
The same letters can hide unrelated roots. In hippopotamus and Mesopotamia, potam- is Greek potamos "river": the "river horse" (with hippos "horse") and the land between rivers. Old English glossed the animal as saehengest, "sea-stallion." In potential and potent, pot- is Latin posse "to be able." The Potomac is a river, but its name has nothing to do with potamos; it comes from the Algonquian name of a village and people recorded as Patawomeck.

Homo- is a double trap. Greek homos means "same": homogeneous (of the same kind), homonym (same name). Latin homo means "human being": homicide, Homo sapiens (named by Linnaeus in 1758), and homage, a vassal's declaration that he was his lord's man. Homosexual, coined by the writer Karl-Maria Kertbeny in a private letter of 1868 and published in pamphlets in 1869, uses the Greek: "same-sex." It has nothing to do with the Latin word for human.

Helicopter splits as helico- + -pter, from Greek helix, helik- "spiral" and pteron "wing," the name the French inventor Gustave de Ponton d'Amécourt gave his model in 1861. English speakers reanalyzed it as heli + copter, producing helipad and quadcopter, and its heli- has nothing to do with Greek helios "sun," as in heliocentric. The same pteron gives pterodactyl, "wing-finger," named by Georges Cuvier in 1809 for a reptile whose wing stretched from one very long finger.

concepts.title: Hybrids and the Purists
concepts.contentHtml:
A hybrid joins roots from two languages. Television is Greek tele "far" + Latin visio "seeing." The Russian engineer Constantin Perskyi is credited with coining it in a paper read in Paris in August 1900. C. P. Scott, editor of the Manchester Guardian, is often quoted as saying that no good would come of a word half Greek and half Latin. Quote Investigator traced Scott's complaint about the word to a 1955 recollection by Kenneth Adam, and found the famous punchline first in a 1956 article by Bernard Levin, long after Scott's death in 1932. Treat the quip as an attribution, not a record.

Hybrids are everywhere. Automobile joins Greek autos "self" to Latin mobilis "movable"; French formed it, and English took the noun in the 1890s. Bicycle (1868) is Latin bi- + Greek kyklos "circle, wheel." Sociology, put into circulation by Auguste Comte in 1838, is Latin socius "companion" + Greek -logia. Hypersonic and appendicitis, from earlier lessons, are hybrids too.

Purists objected for generations. In A Dictionary of Modern English Usage (1926), H. W. Fowler printed a list of hybrids "of which all readers will condemn some, & some all," including bureaucracy (French bureau + Greek -kratia "rule") and speedometer (English speed + Greek metron "measure"). Usage ignored him; words survive when they are useful. For a decoder a hybrid is no harder than a pure word, because each part keeps its own meaning.

concepts.title: Folk Etymologies, and How to Decode Safely
concepts.contentHtml:
A folk etymology is a satisfying story that the evidence does not support. Sincere is often said to come from sine cera, "without wax," because dishonest sculptors supposedly hid cracks with wax. Versions of the tale go back to the early 1600s, but the Oxford English Dictionary rejects it. The real source is Latin sincerus "clean, pure, unmixed," whose own origin is uncertain. History is not "his story": it is Greek historia, "inquiry," from histor, one who knows, a judge. Herodotus opened his book as the display of his historie, his inquiry. "Herstory" is a deliberate pun, not a correction.

Posh carries the best-known acronym myth, "Port Out, Starboard Home," supposedly stamped on tickets for shaded cabins on the voyage to India. The adjective appears in print during the First World War, while the acronym story surfaces only in the 1930s. P&O has denied the term existed, and no ticket stamped with it has ever been produced. A possible ancestor is London slang posh "money," recorded from 1830, though that link is unproven. Acronym etymologies for old words are almost always wrong: the word acronym dates only from 1943, and making words from initials was uncommon before the 20th century.

The decoder's method, then: split the word into prefix, root and suffix; match each piece to a known meaning; check a dictionary that cites dated evidence; and distrust lookalikes and stories that are too neat.
